alt: The finished carved bass hanger with its chrome hook, the oil tin, cloth and a curl of shavings on the workbench
scene:
THE SERIES LOOK, IDENTICAL IN EVERY IMAGE OF THIS ARTICLE: the SAME single object throughout, a WOODEN CLOTHES HANGER carved from one solid board of warm cherry hardwood, 40 cm wide and 16 cm tall, its shape EXACTLY the hanger in image 1: a low wide triangle with long gently sloping shoulders and a straight flat bottom EDGE, and a small rounded raised boss at the top centre with one small drilled hole through it. IT IS ONE SINGLE SOLID PANEL CUT FROM ONE BOARD: there is NO separate bar, NO round rod, NO dowel, NO trouser rail and NO gap of any kind below the carving. The bottom edge is simply where the panel ends. Sunk into the triangular face, inside a raised bead border that follows the outline, is the EXACT carved scene from image 1 and no other: ONE large largemouth bass in profile, head to the LEFT, mouth closed, broad tail to the RIGHT, its body crossing the middle of the panel, swimming through a tangle of submerged tree roots and bare branches that reach in from both lower corners, over a dark finely stippled water ground. Same fish, same pose, same roots, every time. The wood is warm satin cherry, hand-rubbed, never gloss, never painted; the recessed ground is a few shades darker than the raised carving so the bass stands out; straight grain runs the LONG way across the hanger. Where a hook appears it is ALWAYS the same one: a slim polished chrome SWIVEL hanger hook about 10 cm tall, a smooth open question-mark curve with a small ball tip, a short threaded shank, screwed vertically into the boss.
PHOTOGRAPHY, THE SAME IN EVERY FRAME: rich warm cinematic lodge lighting, a low golden key light from the left and deep soft shadow on the right, dark timber and muted greens in the background, shallow depth of field with the carving tack sharp and the background melting away, fine dust motes in the light, colour grade warm amber and deep brown. Magazine quality, editorial, never flat, never a phone snapshot. ABSOLUTELY NO LETTERS, WORDS, NUMBERS, LOGOS, LABELS OR CARVED TEXT anywhere in the picture.
COVER SHOT, THE OPENING PICTURE OF THE ARTICLE, DIFFERENT FROM EVERY OTHER FRAME: NO wardrobe, NO rail, NO coat, NO jacket anywhere. The FINISHED oiled hanger, hook fitted, stands UPRIGHT and leaning back slightly against a dark timber wall at the back of the workbench, facing the camera square on so the whole triangular panel and the bass fill the middle of the picture. Laid out low in front of it and softly out of focus: the small plain tin of oil with its lid off, a folded cream cloth with a warm stain on it, one long curl of cherry shaving, and a second chrome hook still unused lying beside them. Deep warm lantern light from the left, the background falling to near black, one shaft catching the chrome of the hook. Still life, editorial, magazine cover quality.

TWO DIFFERENT SURFACES ON ONE PANEL, SPLIT BY A VERTICAL LINE DOWN THE MIDDLE OF THE PICTURE. This is a close view of the middle of the hanger only, not the whole hanger. THE LEFT HALF OF THE PICTURE: the carving is completely finished, silky and rounded, the bass's head, eye, gill plate and scales sharp, the roots smooth and polished by the cutter. THE RIGHT HALF OF THE PICTURE: the very same carving but LEFT AS ROUGH MACHINE STEPS, built entirely from flat horizontal shelves stacked one above another like a contour model or a stepped wedding cake, six or seven visible steps with hard square edges between them, no smooth surfaces at all, no fine detail, the fish barely recognisable as a blocky stepped mound. Exactly on the dividing line, a slender tapered ball nose router bit is cutting downward, held in a visible collet, turning the steps on the right into the smooth carving on the left, with a small cone of pale dust at its tip. Hard low golden light from the left so every step on the right throws a black shadow.

EASING THE EDGE WITH A ROUNDOVER BIT. The bare sanded hanger is clamped face up on the bench, one long shoulder edge overhanging so it can be worked. A small compact HAND-HELD PALM ROUTER sits on the panel, gripped by both hands, and in its base is a bearing-guided ROUNDOVER BIT: a small carbide cutter with a concave quarter-circle profile and a shiny steel BALL BEARING below it that rides against the edge of the wood. It is cutting along the outside edge of the shoulder, turning the sharp square corner into a soft rounded one; a fine curl of cherry peels away and a little heap of pale dust sits behind the cut. The part of the edge ALREADY ROUNDED, to the left, is visibly soft and catches the light along its curve; the part still to come, to the right, is still a hard square corner. Tight three-quarter view down the edge, the bearing and the rounded profile clearly readable. Warm low light from the left.
